title: AI Sentiment Analysis Accuracy: What Vendors Disclose (2026)
summary: AI sentiment analysis accuracy claims rarely come with a test behind them. We read 16 vendors' pages and built a checklist and a test you can run yourself.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** When a social listening vendor touts AI sentiment analysis accuracy, ask which metric, which posts, who measured it and when. On the pages we opened in October 2026, 8 of 16 vendors published an accuracy figure, but none paired the test set with an independent check, and we found no current independent head-to-head against human labels. Require the disclosure checklist below, then test each vendor on a shared set of posts you label yourself.


A headline number fits on a slide. The test behind it usually does not.


If you are choosing a social listening platform, AI sentiment analysis accuracy is probably on your scorecard, and every vendor claims to do well. The figures use different metrics, data and years, so they cannot be lined up. Pick on the wrong one and your alerts and reports inherit the error.


This post is a disclosure audit, not a ranking. We read the public sentiment pages of 16 vendors on 2026-10-14 and recorded what each states about accuracy. Then we built a ten-item checklist and a test you can run yourself. For the basics, see[what AI sentiment analysis is](https://syncly.app/blog/what-is-ai-sentiment-analysis-social-listening) ; for what each vendor's sentiment model reads, see this[seven-platform comparison](https://syncly.app/blog/best-social-listening-tools-ai-sentiment-analysis) .


## What do vendors publish about AI sentiment analysis accuracy?


Most publish a headline figure but not the test behind it. Of the 16 vendors we read, 8 state an accuracy figure; among current pages only Brand24 names a metric type with a dataset size, and none cites an independent evaluator.


Every figure below is vendor-reported, measured on its own basis and not comparable with any other. Years on undated pages are the year we read them.

Read the table as claims, not a leaderboard. Publishing less does not make a vendor less accurate, and publishing more does not make it more accurate. Three of the eight rest on dated pages (Meltwater 2019, Talkwalker 2019, Awario 2023).


The other eight (BrandMentions, Determ, Keyhole, NetBase Quid, Onclusive, Pulsar, Sked and Sprout Social) published no figure of their own on the pages we opened.


Descriptions also drift within one vendor. Brandwatch's current Listen help lists 40 language entries and a transformer model, while its 2022 blog cited 44 languages and transfer learning. (Source:[Brandwatch help, 2026](https://social-media-management-help.brandwatch.com/en/articles/12767975-sentiment-and-emotion-analysis) ;[Brandwatch blog, 2022](https://www.brandwatch.com/blog/data-science-behind-brandwatchs-new-sentiment-analysis/) , dated)


## Is there independent evidence on social listening sentiment accuracy?


Almost none, and nothing current. We found one public multi-vendor comparison, a 2019 study by Publicis Groupe's social intelligence unit, which measured how often five vendors agreed with each other, not how often they were right.


The study ran in August 2019 with one English query on IPA craft beer. It compared Crimson Hexagon, NetBase, Talkwalker, Sysomos and YouScan, and says it was not meant to explore overall accuracy. (Source:[Social Intelligence Lab, 2019 study, 2025 write-up](https://thesocialintelligencelab.turtl.co/story/social-listening-head-to-head/?accessible) , dated)


Of 1,185 unique tweets, 496 appeared in three or more vendors' data. On those, 44% got the same label from every vendor, 50% had a vendor veer slightly, and 6% had one veer significantly. (Source:[Social Intelligence Lab, 2019](https://www.thesilab.com/resource/social-listening-head-to-head-comparing-data-volumes-and-sentiment-analysis-across-vendors-free-download) )


The vendors responded: Brandwatch and Meltwater said the study used earlier platforms since merged into new products, and YouScan said models balance precision and recall differently. It is a 2019, English-only, one-topic study with export-limited samples, so it is not a benchmark of today's tools.


Academic work tests models, not products; none of it names a commercial listening platform as the system under test:


-


**SemEval-2017 Task 4 (2017, dated):** the best English systems on three-class tweet polarity reached 0.681 macro-averaged recall. (Source:[Rosenthal et al., 2017](https://aclanthology.org/S17-2088.pdf) )


-


**Mozetic et al. (2016, dated):** English tweet annotators agreed at Krippendorff's alpha 0.613; the classifier reached 0.516. (Source:[Mozetic et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4858191/) )


-


**Rohde et al. (2025):** 195 trials from 20 Twitter studies pooled to 0.80 accuracy (95% CI 0.76-0.84). (Source:[Rohde et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09728) )


-


**Castro et al. (2019, dated):** on 690 TV-show clips, text plus video beat the best single modality by 4.2 F points speaker-dependent (12.9% relative error reduction, best case) but only 0.4 points (1.1%) speaker-independent. (Source:[Castro et al., 2019](https://aclanthology.org/P19-1455.pdf) )


## How should you read an AI sentiment analysis accuracy number?


Only alongside its metric, class scheme, dataset and labeler agreement. When neutral posts dominate, plain accuracy rewards a model that does little, so SemEval scored tweets on macro-averaged recall and the 2025 meta-analysis calls overall accuracy often misleading.


**Macro-F1** : the average of per-class F1 scores (each balancing precision and recall), so a rare class such as negative posts counts as much as the neutral majority. (Source:[scikit-learn documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.precision_recall_fscore_support.html) )


Four things change what a number means:


-


**Class balance.** In the Publicis data, 61% of tweets every vendor labeled alike were neutral, and the authors call more than 70% neutral common (Source:[Social Intelligence Lab, 2019](https://thesocialintelligencelab.turtl.co/story/social-listening-head-to-head/?accessible) ). Our hypothetical: with 70% neutral, 20% positive and 10% negative posts, labeling everything neutral scores 70% accuracy but 33.3% macro-recall and finds no negatives.


-


**Human agreement ceiling.** The Mozetic authors treat annotator agreement as an approximate upper bound on classifier performance (Source:[Mozetic et al., 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4858191/) , dated). Brandwatch's help page says humans agree about 80% on tweets without naming a study (Source:[Brandwatch help, 2026](https://social-media-management-help.brandwatch.com/en/articles/12767975-sentiment-and-emotion-analysis) ), and Castro's sarcasm labelers started at kappa 0.1463, so a 95% claim needs labeler agreement beside it.


-


**Dataset.** In one study, GPT-3.5 reached 91.9 three-class accuracy on a product-review dataset and 60.1 on a Twitter dataset, on test sets balanced across classes, which real listening data is not. (Source:[Krugmann and Hartmann, 2024](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s40547-024-00143-4.pdf) )


-


**Label definition.** Sentiment toward what? YouScan scores toward your monitoring subject and Sked adds a mixed class, so Brand24's macro-F1 and YouScan's positive-and-negative figure cannot share a scale. (Source:[YouScan, 2025](https://help.youscan.io/en/articles/642044-how-youscan-identifies-post-sentiment) ;[Sked, 2026](https://help.skedsocial.com/how-does-sentiment-analysis-work-in-social-listening-on-sked) )


## Which 10 disclosures should you require from a vendor?


Require ten disclosures, from the figure and its metric to uncertainty signals. Here is our suggested checklist.


1.


**Figure and metric type** (accuracy, macro-F1, per-class recall). Plain accuracy is inflated by a dominant neutral class.


2.


**Test set** : size, platforms, languages, window, class scheme and balance. Balanced sets overstate real-data performance.


3.


**Provenance** : who measured, when, on which model version, with any independent check. Figures age.


4.


**Languages** : the evaluated list, per-language results and behavior outside it. Accuracy varies by language.


5.


**Model type and change log** : rules, machine learning, neural network or LLM. The family predicts failure modes.


6.


**Hard cases** : handling of sarcasm, negation, emoji, slang and mixed opinions, where humans disagree most.


7.


**Human correction** : whether an override retrains the model, and its scope.


8.


**Unit of analysis** : post, comment, entity or aspect. One label per post averages away opposing opinions.


9.


**Media inputs** : what is read from video, audio and images, and how media-only posts are handled.


10.


**Uncertainty signals** : a confidence score or unclassified share, showing what the dashboard leaves out.


We marked each vendor per item as disclosed (stated specifically and currently), partly (vague, dated before 2024 or incomplete) or not published on the pages we opened. This counts disclosures on those pages only; it is not an accuracy score or a ranking.

## What is documented about sentiment on short-form video?


Little. Sprout Social leaves media-only posts unclassified, Emplifi scores TikTok comments rather than the video, and among the pages we opened only Pulsar documents speech-to-text and on-screen text feeding sentiment. None publishes a video-specific accuracy figure.


-


**Sprout Social:** a message with only an image, video or link and no text lands in the unclassified bucket, so a caption-less clip gets no label. (Source:[Sprout Social, 2026](https://support.sproutsocial.com/hc/en-us/articles/18814496971533) )


-


**Emplifi:** sentiment applies to comments on TikTok and YouTube videos, Facebook comments and X mentions; the unit is the comment, not the video. (Source:[Emplifi, 2026](https://docs.emplifi.io/platform/latest/home/use-sentiment-analysis-to-understand-your-audience) )


-


**Pulsar:** a June 2026 vendor guide says voice-to-text transcribes TikTok, Instagram, X and YouTube content, with image captioning and OCR feeding the same models, but gives no accuracy figure for these inputs. (Source:[Pulsar, 2026](https://www.pulsarplatform.com/guides/understanding-sentiment-analysis-detailed-guide-b2b) )


Nor do the pages say what share of TikTok, Reels or Shorts posts has a transcript or on-screen text available to the model. The multimodal sarcasm result above used TV dialogue, not social posts. For caption-based gaps, read[what text-only listening misses](https://syncly.app/blog/short-form-video-mentions-social-listening-misses) .


## How can you test sentiment accuracy yourself?


Run every vendor on the same shared list of posts, have two blind labelers label a sample from written rules, and score each vendor with a confusion matrix and per-class precision and recall, not one accuracy number. This is our suggested protocol, not a standard.


1.


**Decide what is scored.** Sentiment toward which brand, at post, comment or aspect level? For video, the labeler sees the whole clip with sound and on-screen text.


2.


**Use one query, window and shared post list.** Ask for per-post exports before a trial. In the Publicis study only 496 of 1,185 harvested tweets appeared in three or more vendors' data, and some vendors capped exports (2019, dated).


3.


**Stratify the sample.** Draw a random sample, split by platform, language and product line, then add hard cases: sarcasm, mixed opinions, comparisons, emoji-only posts and no-caption video.


4.


**Write labeling rules first.** Cover the target, neutral, mixed, sponsored posts and sarcasm, then pilot on 30-50 posts. In Castro et al., annotator agreement began at kappa 0.1463, rose to 0.2326 after reconciliation and reached 0.5877 on the second batch; beauty teams can start from our[skincare complaint categories](https://syncly.app/blog/tiktok-comment-sentiment-skincare) .


5.


**Label blind with two people.** Compute percent agreement and Cohen's kappa (Fleiss for three or more), and have a third person settle disagreements. (Source:[McHugh, 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3900052) , dated)


6.


**Score each vendor.** Report the confusion matrix, per-class precision and recall, macro-F1, the unclassified share and sentiment inversions (positive called negative or the reverse).


7.


**Compare on the same posts, then re-test.** For two vendors on one fixed set that each run once, McNemar's test is the acceptable choice (Source:[Dietterich, 1998](https://web.engr.oregonstate.edu/~tgd/publications/dietterich-approximate-statistical-tests-nc1998.pdf) , dated). Repeat after four to eight weeks or a model change.


**Margin of error** : the uncertainty around an accuracy estimate from a labeled sample, which shrinks as the sample grows. At 100 labeled posts it is about ±10 points at 95% confidence in the worst case, and about ±5 points at 385 (standard normal-approximation formula for a proportion; Source:[MacEwan University](https://openbooks.macewan.ca/introstats/chapter/10-4-margin-of-error-and-sample-size-calculation-for-proportion/) ). A 100-post check is a smoke test: it can catch gross failures but cannot rank vendors within several points of each other.


We claim no universal right sample size, and the formula covers one overall proportion. A rare class needs more: with 10% negative posts, a random 385 holds about 38 negatives, so negative recall stays noisy.


## Key Takeaways


-


Eight of 16 vendors gave a sentiment accuracy figure, but none of the pages we opened paired the test set with provenance.


-


Vendor figures use different metrics, classes and data, so they are not comparable, and less disclosure does not mean lower accuracy.


-


The only public multi-vendor comparison we found is a 2019 study of vendor agreement, not accuracy against human labels.


-


Require the 10-item checklist, and treat a 100-post hand-label check as a smoke test with about ±10 points of uncertainty.


-


For short-form video, ask what is read: caption, comments, transcript or on-screen text.


Vendors publish numbers, but rarely the provenance that makes a number usable, and no current independent benchmark fills the gap. That is not evidence that any one vendor is weak. The evaluation work moves to you.


The better question is not which platform claims the highest accuracy but which will show its work on your posts.
